title: The Lit Windows of Amberlight
logline: When the shut rooms of Amberlight House light their windows beside the parish schoolroom after six years dark, the parish decides its new master is hiding a madwoman, when in truth he is hiding his own kindness.
promise: A shuttered house, a family that will not explain itself, and a perfectly ordinary reason for all of it, arrived at only after the whole parish has guessed wrong.

cast.name: Miss Eliza Combe
cast.station: keeps her late mother's dressmaking trade, taking work through the draper's counter; no fortune beyond her needle
cast.want: to be dealt with as a tradeswoman of skill and honesty, not managed or pitied by her betters
cast.appearance: Twenty-six, slight and quick-moving, dark hair pinned under a plain cap, a pincushion always at her wrist.
cast.dress: A serviceable brown stuff gown with a clean white apron, sleeves turned back for work.
cast.voice_note: brisk and plain-spoken, sharpest when she feels looked down on

cast.name: Mr Ambrose Calder
cast.station: trustee for his young cousin's bequest from the late Sir Edward Marchmont's estate; holds the main rooms of Amberlight House by the Marchmont family's leave; a modest independence of his own
cast.want: to protect his young cousin from parish gossip about her broken engagement without having to explain the family's grief to anyone
cast.appearance: Thirty-five, tall and spare, weathered from outdoor riding, with close-cropped grey-flecked hair and a guarded, unsmiling face.
cast.dress: A dark green coat of good cloth but no ornament, mud still on his boots from the road.
cast.voice_note: clipped and formal, drops the guard only when his cousin is frightened

cast.name: Miss Cecily Daunt
cast.station: orphaned ward, heiress to a separate bequest left by the late Sir Edward Marchmont; no Marchmont by name
cast.want: to be left to mourn quietly until she can face the parish without shame
cast.appearance: Nineteen, slight and fair, with red-rimmed eyes and hands that twist constantly at a black ribbon.
cast.dress: Deep mourning black, unrelieved but for a thin strand of jet beads.
cast.voice_note: soft and halting, quick to apologise for her own tears

cast.name: Mrs Honoria Pike
cast.station: widow of a naval surgeon; three hundred a year and a house on the green
cast.want: to be first with the news, and proven right about it
cast.appearance: Short and broad, with grey hair pinned severely under a lace cap, and small quick eyes set in a round weathered face.
cast.dress: Black bombazine with a plain white fichu, ten years out of fashion and immaculately kept.
cast.voice_note: warm, talks too much, never doubts herself

cast.name: Mrs Hale
cast.station: draper's wife; keeps the counter of the circulating library above the shop
cast.want: to pass on exactly what she has heard, to everyone, the moment she has heard it
cast.appearance: Round-faced and pink, with spectacles pushed up into hair the colour of weak tea.
cast.dress: A striped apron over her gown, never removed even to serve customers upstairs.
cast.voice_note: reports gossip as news and news as gossip, precise and without malice

cast.name: Mr Silas Rowe
cast.station: curate of Amberlight; eighty a year and no expectations. Oversees the parish schoolroom in the east wing of Amberlight House.
cast.want: to keep his schoolroom warm and his scholars out of the shut rooms next door
cast.appearance: Tall and thin, dark hair worn slightly too long, with the stoop of a man used to low doorways and a face that gives away more than he intends.
cast.dress: Worn black coat, carefully brushed, and linen that has been turned at the cuffs.

chapters.title: Lights Above the Schoolroom
beats: Dismissing the children from the east-wing schoolroom at dusk one late October day in 1818, Mr Rowe sees lamps lit in the main rooms of Amberlight House, shut since 1812, and hears a bolt shot somewhere above the long room.

At the draper's next morning Mrs Hale reports that a Mr Ambrose Calder came by night chaise as trustee for a young cousin, by leave of the Marchmont family, who still have not come into the parish themselves.
Eliza Combe, who takes her dressmaking through the draper's counter, is handed a note from Calder ordering full mourning for 'Miss Daunt' within the week, without one word of courtesy.
Mrs Pike declares that a madwoman is being kept under lock, and urges Eliza to look about her when she goes up, since a dressmaker goes where no caller is admitted.

chapters.title: The Measuring
beats: Calder receives Eliza in the cold front hall, refuses to let her see Miss Daunt, and hands her an old gown to work from instead.
Eliza tells him a tradeswoman is owed the civility of any customer, and Calder answers that her business is cloth, not his family's affairs.
Through a part-open door Eliza glimpses Cecily Daunt in black, clutching a packet of letters, plainly grieving and not raving.
Calder abruptly cancels the order, presses double the fee into her hand and shows her out, and Eliza walks home certain she has been paid for her silence.

chapters.title: An Account Settled
beats: By Saturday the parish has the madwoman whole: Mrs Pike adds a chained door, and Mrs Hale repeats word for word what two scholars say they heard crying through the schoolroom wall.
Eliza finds the cloth debt her late mother left at the draper's marked paid, and Mrs Hale says a gentleman's man settled it in coin and would give no name.
Eliza knows the hand on the receipt for the hand of Calder's curt order, and walks up the lane meaning to throw the money back at him.
She finds the front door standing open, and hears from upstairs a fall and a man's voice calling a name in open fear.

chapters.title: What the House Hid
beats: Eliza runs up and finds Cecily fainted beside a trunk of letters, with Calder kneeling over her and every coldness gone out of him.
Revived, Cecily tells Eliza that her betrothed was killed in a riding accident in the spring, and that his family now say openly she trapped him, so she came where no one knew her face.
Calder admits he paid Eliza's debt because cancelling the order had wronged her, and kept his name off it because any open kindness from the house would set the parish asking why the house was lit.
Cecily asks to be let into the parish properly at last, and below them Mrs Pike's voice is heard at the open door, with Mrs Hale behind her.

chapters.title: Every Window Lit
beats: Eliza and Calder meet Mrs Pike and Mrs Hale in the hall and tell them the plain truth of a death, a mourning and a cruel family, which ends the madwoman story where it stands.
Mrs Pike declares she always suspected sorrow rather than sin, and at once announces that she foresaw an understanding between Eliza and Calder, which Mrs Hale will repeat exactly.
On Monday Cecily, in mourning Eliza has now made for her properly, comes through to the schoolroom with Mr Rowe and offers to hear the youngest scholars read.
At dusk Eliza and Calder walk down the lane and give each other the apology neither offered before, while every window of Amberlight House stands lit behind them, the schoolroom's included.

Move the story to late autumn 1818 so it agrees with the series bible: Amberlight House stood empty from spring 1812 until summer 1817, and since summer 1817 its old east wing has been the parish schoolroom, fitted at the estate's charge. The rest of the house stayed shut until now.

- Cast: keep Miss Eliza Combe as protagonist, unchanged. Keep the trustee as love interest but give him a new first name (Nathaniel is already used in this parish). Keep the grieving young cousin, but she must not carry the Marchmont surname; give her a new surname, and make her a ward whose bequest came from the late Sir Edward Marchmont's estate. The trustee holds the main block of the house for her by leave of the Marchmont family, who still have not moved in themselves. Ages of recurring characters move forward one year from the bible's 1817 ages.
- Mr Silas Rowe is married by 1818; his wife is Mrs Rowe (formerly Miss Judith Vane). If she appears, copy her bible entry and call her Mrs Rowe. Do not give Mr Rowe arrears "from the Marchmont living" — a curate is paid by the rector, not the patron. Drop the arrears entirely.
- Put Mrs Hale, the draper's wife who keeps the library counter, into the cast as the channel the gossip runs through, alongside Mrs Pike. Eliza's dressmaking takes work through the draper's rather than competing with it.

Replace these wholesale: the chapters and their beats. Five chapters, 3 to 4 concrete beats each — things that happen, not moods.

Story requirements for the new chapters:
- Use the schoolroom as the gothic contrast: children's voices in the lit east wing by day, the shuttered main rooms by night. Mr Rowe teaches or oversees the school there, which is how the parish first learns the main rooms are occupied.
- The trustee's secret kindness stays the heart of it, but the parish must NOT credit Mrs Pike with an anonymous payment, and there is no anonymous payment to Mr Rowe. Mrs Pike's wrong guess is the madwoman. Eliza is the one who traces the kindness back to the trustee herself, through her own settled account.
- No disputed will plot and no apothecary's records as evidence. The cousin's grief and a broken engagement remain the hidden truth.
